structure.title: A stranger recognised
structure.text: Arrivals establish separated family members and a city where people seem to remember events the newcomers never experienced.

structure.title: Confusion accumulates
structure.text: Domestic, financial, and public encounters repeat the mistaken identities until several explanations must be tested together.

people.name: The two Antipholuses
people.text: Twin brothers separated in a shipwreck as babies, one raised in Syracuse and one in Ephesus, both now in Ephesus on the same day.

people.name: The two Dromios
people.text: Their twin servants, separated in the same wreck, who keep being sent on errands by the wrong master and beaten for the mix-ups.

people.name: Adriana
people.text: The wife of the Antipholus of Ephesus, impatient with her husband's absences, who takes the wrong twin home to dinner.

context.title: Who knows which twin
context.text: The audience's knowledge exceeds most characters'. Keeping the two households distinct makes the misunderstandings easier to enjoy.

context.title: Farce with consequences
context.text: Mistakes concern marriage, debt, and legal security. Physical comedy does not make every threatened loss imaginary.
context.takeaway: Notice what each person could lose.

notice.why: Money and possessions make mistaken identity materially consequential.
Contradictory evidence threatens confidence in one's own experience.

opening: A stranger arrives in Ephesus and discovers that people know his name, expect his money, and hold him responsible for things he has never done. Somewhere in the city is the identical twin he has lost, accompanied by a servant who also has an identical twin. Shakespeare makes the confusion wonderfully excessive, then lets it disturb things that matter: a wife's trust, a merchant's reputation, a man's confidence that he is sane. Everyone has evidence, and almost nobody has an explanation that fits it.
